word:greek-nt:G0018.explanation: Agathos means good in nature—intrinsically good, whether or not it is recognized. It can describe a person, a thing, or an action as good.

word:greek-nt:G0061.explanation: Agra means catching or a catch.

word:greek-nt:G0186.explanation: This word describes something unswerving or unwavering—steady rather than turning aside or changing direction. It expresses firmness and constancy, especially when a person or commitment must remain settled. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 10:23. The word itself gives the sense of holding firmly and consistently, while the surrounding verse determines exactly how that steadfastness is applied there.

word:greek-nt:G0216.explanation: Alalos means unable to speak, or mute.

word:greek-nt:G0263.explanation: This word describes something that does not fade or lose its lasting quality: “never fading” or “unfading.” It presents what is being described as enduring rather than temporary or subject to decay. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament corpus, in 1 Peter 1:4. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is something that remains unfaded and enduring.

word:greek-nt:G0322.explanation: Anadeiknymi means to show clearly or appoint.

word:greek-nt:G0450.explanation: Anistēmi means to rise or get up. It can also mean to raise someone up.

word:greek-nt:G0524.explanation: This word means “to become callous” or “to lose all sensitivity,” describing a person who has become emotionally and morally unresponsive. It points to a deep hardening in which a person no longer reacts with proper feeling or concern. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Ephesians 4:19, so its broader use cannot be traced through multiple passages. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea is the loss of inward sensitivity.

word:greek-nt:G0591.explanation: Apodidōmi means to give back or return, to render what is due, and to pay what is owed.

word:greek-nt:G0717.explanation: Harmagedon is a place-name, rendered Armageddon in English.

word:greek-nt:G0836.explanation: Aulos means a flute or pipe.

word:greek-nt:G0915.explanation: Barbaros means a foreigner or barbarian. The word can describe people contrasted with Greeks, or a speaker whose language another person does not understand.

word:greek-nt:G0959.explanation: Bernikē is the personal name Bernice.

word:greek-nt:G1044.explanation: This word means “gangrene,” a destructive condition in which body tissue decays and the damage may spread. It is a noun naming a serious physical process rather than an action or character trait. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Timothy 2:17. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself presents something harmful that advances and causes increasing damage.

word:greek-nt:G1088.explanation: Gerōn means an old man or old person.

word:greek-nt:G1170.explanation: Deina means “so-and-so,” a certain person whose name is known but not used.

word:greek-nt:G1192.explanation: Derma means the skin or hide of an animal. It can refer to sheep skins and goat skins worn as clothing.

word:greek-nt:G1202.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “prisoner” or “prisoners”—a person or group held in custody. It is a noun describing people who are detained rather than free to leave. In this Greek New Testament corpus, it appears twice, both times in Acts 27, referring to prisoners being transported during Paul’s voyage. The plural wording indicates more than one detained person in each occurrence. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the specific scene, but the word itself identifies those under guard or confinement.

word:greek-nt:G1413.explanation: Dynastēs means a ruler or potentate, someone who holds authority.

word:greek-nt:G1538.explanation: Hekastos means each one or every one, pointing to members of a group individually rather than only collectively.

word:greek-nt:G1541.explanation: This word describes someone or something that is a hundred years old. It expresses an age of one hundred years rather than a general idea of being old. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Romans 4:19. Because the word occurs only there and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise role in that sentence must be understood from the passage itself; its basic meaning remains a specific age: “a hundred years old.”

word:greek-nt:G1620.explanation: Ektithemi means to set forth, explain, or expound. It can also describe putting out or exposing a child.

word:greek-nt:G1725.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “before.” It indicates that something comes earlier than another thing or is positioned in front of someone or something, depending on the sentence. It appears two times in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 1:8 and Acts 8:21. Its basic idea is relational: it places a person, action, or circumstance ahead of another in time or position. The surrounding verse determines which sense is intended in a particular occurrence.

word:greek-nt:G1769.explanation: This word means “speechless,” describing someone who is unable to speak. It presents silence as a condition affecting a person’s ability to express words aloud, rather than simply choosing not to speak. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 9:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on being without speech. The same meaning is reflected in the English rendering “speechless.”

word:greek-nt:G1862.explanation: This word means “a promise”: a declared assurance about something that will be given or accomplished. It is a noun, so it names the promise itself rather than the act of promising. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Peter—once in the plural and once in the singular. Its basic meaning remains the same whether referring to several promises or one particular promise. The surrounding passage determines what promised matter is in view in each verse.

word:greek-nt:G1880.explanation: Epanerchomai means to return or come back again.

word:greek-nt:G1967.explanation: Epiousios means daily or for the day.

word:greek-nt:G1989.explanation: Epistellō means to write or send by letter.

word:greek-nt:G2096.explanation: This word is the personal name “Eve.” It functions as a proper name, identifying Eve when she is mentioned in the Greek New Testament. The word occurs twice in this corpus, once in 2 Corinthians and once in 1 Timothy, and both occurrences are rendered “Eve.” Because it is a name rather than a general description, its meaning is primarily identification: it points to the individual called Eve. The surrounding verse supplies the specific purpose of mentioning her in each passage.

word:greek-nt:G2139.explanation: This word describes something “easily entangling” or “thwarting”—something that readily ensnares a person or gets in the way. It points to an obstacle that can hinder movement or progress, rather than simply describing ordinary difficulty. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 12:1. The precise force of the word in that verse is understood through its surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic sense is something that entangles or obstructs.

word:greek-nt:G2175.explanation: Euōdia means a sweet smell or fragrance.

word:greek-nt:G2210.explanation: Ἐζημιώθην means to forfeit or lose something.

word:greek-nt:G2434.explanation: Hilasmos means an atoning sacrifice or propitiation.

word:greek-nt:G2481.explanation: “Perhaps” expresses possibility rather than certainty. It presents something as a consideration that may or may not happen, without declaring it definite. This Greek New Testament word occurs once, in Luke 20:13, so its normal meaning is established from that single occurrence and the gloss “perhaps,” while the surrounding verse supplies its particular force there. It functions as a concise word of uncertainty, leaving room for an outcome or possibility without treating it as assured.

word:greek-nt:G2526.explanation: Katho means “according to,” showing what a statement or judgment is related to. It marks the standard for acceptance: what a person has, rather than what he does not have.

word:greek-nt:G2553.explanation: This Greek New Testament verb means “to endure” or “to suffer trouble.” It describes continuing through hardship rather than escaping or avoiding it. The word can refer generally to undergoing difficulty and remaining steadfast while doing so. It occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, in two letters: twice in 2 Timothy and once in James. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence and situation.

word:greek-nt:G2632.explanation: Katakrino means to condemn, or to judge a person worthy of punishment. The word can describe judging someone worthy of death.

word:greek-nt:G2711.explanation: Katapsycho means to cool. It can also mean to refresh.

word:greek-nt:G2768.explanation: Keras means a horn. It can also name a horn-like projection at the corner of an altar. In symbolic language, a horn can represent strength or power.

word:greek-nt:G2830.explanation: Klydōn means rough or raging water. It can also refer to a wave.

word:greek-nt:G2993.explanation: Laodicea is the name of a city. Scripture identifies an assembly as being in Laodicea.

word:greek-nt:G3073.explanation: Lycia is the name of a region on the southwestern coast of Asia Minor. It functions as a place-name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 27:5. The name identifies a location within the travel account, while the surrounding passage supplies the details of the journey. Thus, its basic meaning is simply “Lycia,” the geographic region named in that verse.

word:greek-nt:G3198.explanation: Melchisedek is a personal name for a king of Salem and priest of God Most High.

word:greek-nt:G3327.explanation: Metabainō means to depart or move from one place to another.

word:greek-nt:G3385.explanation: Mēti means “if not” or “whether at all,” and it can mark a negative question. It can also mean “unless” in a condition.

word:greek-nt:G3521.explanation: Nēsteia means fasting. It can also refer to the day of atonement, called the Fast.

word:greek-nt:G3558.explanation: Notos means the south or a south wind.

word:greek-nt:G3594.explanation: Hodēgeō means to lead or guide.

word:greek-nt:G3679.explanation: Oneidizo means to reproach, revile, or insult someone. It can also describe upbraiding someone for unbelief.

word:greek-nt:G3697.explanation: Hopoios means of what kind or sort.

word:greek-nt:G3723.explanation: Orthōs means rightly. It can also mean correctly.

word:greek-nt:G3756.explanation: Ou means no or not. It negates an expression, as in “will not hurt.”

word:greek-nt:G3828.explanation: Pamphylia is a place-name for a Roman province on the south coast of Asia Minor.

word:greek-nt:G3851.explanation: This word means “to risk”—to take a chance or expose oneself to possible danger or loss. It describes an act of deliberate daring rather than merely facing difficulty. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Philippians 2:30. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the decision to undertake something despite the danger involved.

word:greek-nt:G3972.explanation: Paulos is a personal name, rendered Paul or Paulus.

word:greek-nt:G3990.explanation: Pelekizō means to behead, specifically to cut off the head with an axe.

word:greek-nt:G4021.explanation: Periergos describes meddling or overly curious people and can also refer to magical arts.

word:greek-nt:G4058.explanation: Peristera means a dove. It can also mean a pigeon.

word:greek-nt:G4094.explanation: Pinax means a plate, platter, or dish.

word:greek-nt:G4223.explanation: Puteoli is the name of a place. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Acts 28:13, and English Bible translations preserve it as “Puteoli” rather than translating it as a descriptive word. As a proper name, it identifies a specific location mentioned in the account. The word itself does not describe an action, quality, or spiritual principle; its function is to name the place. The surrounding verse and passage provide the details about what happened there.

word:greek-nt:G4256.explanation: This Greek New Testament verb means to accuse someone, make a charge beforehand, or say that a charge has already been made. It describes the act of bringing an accusation against a person rather than merely noticing a fault. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Romans 3:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is the formal or deliberate raising of an accusation.

word:greek-nt:G4335.explanation: Proseuchē means prayer to God. It can also refer to a place for prayer.

word:greek-nt:G4379.explanation: This word means “to touch,” describing physical contact with someone or something. It is a verb that expresses the act of making contact rather than merely seeing, approaching, or speaking. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 11:46. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is the straightforward action of touching. This word should therefore be understood as an expression of contact.

word:greek-nt:G4397.explanation: Prophetic means uttered by a prophet.

word:greek-nt:G4454.explanation: Pōlos means a colt, a young donkey, or a foal.

word:greek-nt:G4498.explanation: Rhoda is a personal name used to identify an individual, rather than a word expressing an action, quality, or object. It is rendered “Rhoda” and appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 12:13. Because it is a name, its meaning here is primarily identification: it tells the reader who a person is, while the surrounding passage supplies the person’s role and actions. The name itself does not describe a general spiritual principle or idea.

word:greek-nt:G4506.explanation: Rhyomai means to rescue or deliver from danger or destruction.

word:greek-nt:G4573.explanation: Sebazomai means to worship. In one example, it describes worshiping the creature rather than the Creator.

word:greek-nt:G4685.explanation: Spao means to draw or pull, as in drawing a sword.

word:greek-nt:G4829.explanation: This word means “to share” or “to share with,” expressing the act of participating in or receiving something together with others. It describes sharing rather than keeping something solely for oneself, and its wording can point to a shared portion or participation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 9:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is sharing in something with others.

word:greek-nt:G4865.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “to join in a struggle” or “to struggle.” It expresses active participation in difficult effort, emphasizing that someone enters the struggle rather than merely observing it. The wording can describe sharing in a demanding contest or labor with others. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Romans 15:30, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:greek-nt:G4960.explanation: This word means “to correspond” or “to correspond to,” expressing a relationship in which something matches, aligns with, or stands alongside something else. It is a verb describing correspondence rather than naming an object or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Galatians 4:25. The surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain precisely what is being compared there, but the word itself centers on agreement or matching between related things.

word:greek-nt:G4982.explanation: Sōzō means to save or rescue. It can also mean to preserve a life. It can also mean to heal.

word:greek-nt:G5004.explanation: Misery refers to a condition of distress, suffering, or wretchedness. It describes the painful state a person experiences rather than an action they perform. In the Greek New Testament, this word appears twice, rendered “misery” in both occurrences, including Romans 3:16 and James 5:1. Its exact force in either verse is determined by the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the experience of severe hardship or sorrow.

word:greek-nt:G5152.explanation: This Greek New Testament word refers to the “third story,” meaning the third level of a building. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Acts 20:9. The word identifies a location or level rather than expressing an action, quality, or person. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning is a building’s third story.

word:greek-nt:G5215.explanation: The word means “hymn,” referring to a song intended to be sung. It functions as a noun, naming a kind of song rather than an action or a person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16. Its basic meaning is therefore a hymn or sung composition, while the precise role it plays in either verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage.

word:greek-nt:G5259.explanation: Hypo means under. It can also mean by, identifying the person through whom an action occurs, as with baptism by John.

word:greek-nt:G5336.explanation: Phatne means a manger or feeding trough. It can also mean a stall for an animal.

word:greek-nt:G5343.explanation: Pheugō means to flee or escape. It describes leaving a threatened situation, as when Joseph is told to flee because Herod seeks to destroy the child.

word:greek-nt:G5400.explanation: This word refers to a “fearful event” or “fearful thing”—something that causes alarm or dread. It names the frightening occurrence itself rather than describing fear as an emotion felt inwardly. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 21:11. Because the word appears only there and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the passage around it. Its central meaning remains something genuinely alarming or terrifying.

word:greek-nt:G5509.explanation: Chitōn means a tunic or garment.
